source.title: High-dimensional Analysis of Knowledge Distillation: Weak-to-Strong Generalization and Scaling Laws
source.authors: M. E. Ildiz; Halil Alperen Gozeten; Ege Onur Taga; Marco Mondelli; Samet Oymak

page_placements.theme: Weak supervision beating strong training on gold or on the same labels (PGR above 1, OPR above 1)

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests weak-to-strong fine-tuning using a CIFAR-10 ResNet-50 and compares accuracy with weak supervisors and a true-label target, but it does not use or report Burns et al.'s PGR measure.
record.gate_note: The paper's own CIFAR-10 experiment reports weak-to-strong accuracy comparisons for three supervisor sizes. Figure 2a provides the plotted values, while the text states the qualitative comparisons. The numerical two-stage risk experiment in Figure 2b validates the risk characterization but does not compare student performance with the weak supervisor. Results attributed to other work, including the GPT-4/GPT-2 comparison, are not included.
record.test_reason: Section 3.1 and Fig. 2a fine-tune a pretrained ResNet-50 on CIFAR-10 using predictions from three weak 3-layer CNNs. The text reports that students consistently beat their supervisors, which bears on V1 in a vision setting (V6). The rest of the paper is linear-regression theory comparing the student with a true-label target, not with the weak supervisor.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The headline is theoretical: in high-dimensional ridgeless regression, an optimally designed or feature-masked weak surrogate provably lets the student beat training on strong labels with the same data, but cannot improve the scaling-law exponent. The benefit exists only when the target is over-parameterised. In the CIFAR-10 experiment, students beat their CNN supervisors but not the true-label ResNet-50. The authors attribute this to the surrogates not following the optimal feature-selection mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: It fine-tunes a pretrained ResNet50 on weak CNN predictions, but evaluates accuracy rather than Burns et al.'s PGR; it also develops a separate high-dimensional linear-regression risk analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The CIFAR-10 weak-to-strong result is reported across big, medium, and small weak CNN supervisors; all yield students that outperform the supervisor, but none outperform the true-label target.

fits_no_version.finding: In ridgeless over-parameterised regression, a surrogate that masks features with ζi² > 1−Ω gives the target lower asymptotic risk than training on true labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A suitably feature-pruned weak supervisor can make the strong student beat the strong ceiling (PGR above 1) in over-parameterised linear regression.

fits_no_version.finding: When the target is under-parameterised (n > p), no surrogate beats true-label training asymptotically.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains beyond the ceiling require an over-parameterised student.

fits_no_version.finding: Under power-law spectra, the optimal surrogate leaves the excess-risk scaling exponent in n unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak-to-strong (distillation) supervision cannot improve the data scaling law in linear regression.

record.problems: The CIFAR-10 accuracy values are shown only in a plot and are not stated numerically in the text. No PGR values or uncertainty estimates for the plotted comparisons are reported. The vision experiment uses one dataset and one strong-model architecture.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2b's synthetic two-stage risk-versus-theory comparison is omitted because it does not compare student performance with the weak supervisor. Cited findings from other work are omitted.

untested.parts: No PGR values; only qualitative student-over-supervisor statements; no language tasks.
No auxiliary loss, ensembling or loss variants.
Three supervisor sizes are used, but no variation of the gain with size, task or representations is reported. The theory concerns beating true-label training, not PGR.
Not studied. Section 5's distribution shift concerns the risk characterisation, not a PGR drop.
The theory gives conditions for beating the true-label target (Prop. 3), not for beating the supervisor.
Only CIFAR-10 with one strong architecture; no PGR, single run, no uncertainty.

missing.what: Numeric CIFAR-10 accuracies for the three surrogates, the three students and the true-label target, needed to compute PGR; they can only be read off the plot.

record.verdict_notes: The earlier limits_scope labels from r4–r6 are removed: not reaching the strong ceiling is consistent with V1's PGR above 0 and is what Burns et al. report, so it is not a qualification. Design differs from Burns et al.: the surrogates were trained on the CIFAR-10 training split, and the student is then trained on surrogate predictions over the same split (no held-out weak-label split). The setup reports a single run with no error bars. The GPT-4/GPT-2 comparison is cited from Burns et al., not the authors' own result.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports no PGR values; it tests the basic effect with CIFAR-10 accuracy comparisons instead.
No auxiliary confidence loss, weak-supervisor ensemble, or loss-variant gain over naive fine-tuning is tested.
It varies weak-supervisor capacity in one image-classification task, but does not report PGR magnitudes, student-size scaling, or results for NLP, chess, reward modelling, or representations.
No supervisor-checking failure, distribution-shift drop in PGR, or shared-error analysis is reported.
The theory concerns risk in linear regression and does not establish conditions requiring a student to beat its weak supervisor.
The vision test is limited to CIFAR-10 and the models/settings described in the paper.

tranche.reason: The claim-bearing experiment applies weak-label fine-tuning to a new CIFAR-10 CNN-to-ResNet50 setting. Reporting accuracy instead of normalized PGR does not itself introduce a different training method; the separate regression theory compares against true-label training.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v2, dated 27 February 2025. The authors' theoretical improvement concerns the true-label target, requires overparameterization, and is not a guarantee that a student beats its supervisor; optimal unrestricted-surrogate improvement also excludes isotropic covariance.

statements.correction: Pretrained ResNet50; CIFAR-10; three-layer CNN supervisors with 127,094, 58,342 and 28,286 parameters; students outperform each supervisor but underperform the true-label target; exact accuracies figure-only; run count and uncertainty estimates not stated; ICLR venue unverified from supplied text.
statements.problem: The parameter counts and performance comparisons are supported. A single run is not stated; the supplied text also does not establish the ICLR review designation.

statements.correction: Proposition 3: retain features with ζi²<1−Ω, using retained ground-truth coefficients. Proposition 2: for n>p, no surrogate improves asymptotic risk over true-label training. Proposition 6: λi=i^(−α), λiβi²=i^(−β), α,β>1, p→∞; optimal-surrogate and standard-target risks share exponent β−1 when β<2α+1 and 2α when β>2α+1; noise variance must be O(n^(−(β−1))) or O(n^(−2α)), respectively.
statements.problem: The theoretical comparisons are correct, but the scaling statement omits the power-law and noise assumptions required for the stated excess-risk behavior.
